Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Amir is a 38-year-old hairdresser who nearly died two years ago from a catastrophic bacterial infection that spiraled into septic shock. What began as a stubborn cough became a fever that would not break, then a rapid decline that landed him in the ICU for three weeks. He remembers the exact moment a doctor told his family he might not survive—the fluorescent lights flickering, the antiseptic smell so thick it coated his tongue, and a deep, wrenching pain in his chest that felt like something was physically tearing inside him. He survived, but his body never felt safe again.

In the months that followed, Amir tried to return to his life. He went back to work at the salon, but he found himself flinching whenever a client showed him a photo on their phone. Once, a regular customer pulled up a picture of her newborn, and for a split second Amir saw a hospital bassinet instead of a baby—his chest seized, his palms went slick, and he had to excuse himself to the back room. He started avoiding the break room entirely because a coworker had taped a get-well card from Amir’s own hospital stay on the bulletin board, the front showing a generic bouquet that he now associated with sterile waiting rooms. He never asked her to take it down. He just stopped going in there.

Sleep became a kind of ordeal. He would wake from nightmares without a clear image—just the full weight of that terror pressing down on his ribs, his heart hammering, his skin cold with sweat. Sometimes he smelled the ICU again: alcohol wipes, saline, the faint metallic tang of blood. He learned to lie still until the feeling passed, certain that if he moved he would trigger something worse. On nights when the pain came back—a dull ache in the exact spot where the central line had been inserted—he would press his palm to his chest and whisper, *It’s over*, but his body did not believe him.

Amir’s body had become a source of constant vigilance. He felt tense all the time, as though he were bracing for an impact that never came. At the salon, he caught himself scanning the room for exits, for people who looked too pale or too flushed. He started taking his blood pressure on a home monitor every morning, even though his doctor had told him it was unnecessary. The numbers were always normal, but he could not shake the sense that his body was waiting to betray him again. He began to wonder if he was losing his mind—if his reactions since the illness meant something was fundamentally broken in his head. He did not tell anyone. He was a hairdresser, someone who made people feel good about themselves. How could he admit he was terrified of his own skin?

The worst moments came without warning while he was simply standing at his station, cutting hair. He would be mid-sentence, scissors in hand, and then—nothing visual at all—a wave of pure horror would wash through him, leaving him dizzy and short of breath. His client would ask if he was okay, and he would smile, say he just needed water, and retreat to the back room to breathe into his hands. He started booking fewer appointments, taking more days off. His income dropped. His boss, a patient woman, asked if something was wrong. Amir said he was fine.

He avoided medical procedures with a determination that surprised even him. A routine physical became a week-long dread spiral. He cancelled his follow-up with the infectious disease specialist three times. Each time, he told himself he would reschedule tomorrow. Tomorrow never came. The thought of lying on an examination table, of someone touching his chest or drawing blood, made his stomach clench. He had come to believe that his body was an enemy that could never be trusted—that the illness had been a warning, and that if he let his guard down, something worse would happen.

A few weeks ago, a friend posted an old photo on social media—a group shot from before the illness. Amir was in it, healthy, smiling. He stared at the image for a long time, then felt his throat close up. He deleted the app from his phone. That night, he woke from a nightmare gasping, the pain in his chest so real he almost called an ambulance. He did not call. But the next morning, he made an appointment with a therapist who specialized in trauma.

Sitting in the waiting room, Amir is certain of two things: he cannot go on like this, and he is terrified that the therapist will confirm what he already suspects—that he is going crazy, that his body has a secret expiration date, that the illness is only sleeping inside him. He wants to be told he is wrong. He hopes that someone can help him trust his own heartbeat again.
